subQuestions.questionText: The settlement pattern shown in P is best described as a … (Refer to Figure 1.1 — Three rural settlement patterns: P, Q and R in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B nucleated pattern (1 mark)
Pattern P shows tightly clustered houses around a central well/market.

subQuestions.questionText: The pattern shown in R is most likely to develop along … (Refer to Figure 1.1 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A railway lines and rivers (1 mark)
R shows linear development hugging the river/road.

subQuestions.questionText: The pattern shown in Q is typical of … (Refer to Figure 1.1 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C commercial farming areas (1 mark)
Q shows scattered farmhouses on commercial farms.

subQuestions.questionText: A small rural cluster of fewer than approximately 50 inhabitants and offering no services is called a …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B hamlet (1 mark)
Hamlet = smallest rural cluster, fewer than ~50 people, no services.

subQuestions.questionText: The hierarchy of settlements arranged from smallest to largest is …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A hamlet, village, town, city (1 mark)
Standard NSC settlement hierarchy from smallest to largest.

subQuestions.questionText: The minimum number of customers needed to keep a service running is the …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C threshold population (1 mark)
Threshold = minimum customers needed to keep a service viable.

subQuestions.questionText: When two or more cities expand and merge to form one continuous urban area, this is termed a …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B conurbation (1 mark)
Conurbation = merger of two or more cities into one continuous urban area.

subQuestions.questionText: An example of a high-order central place in South Africa is …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C Johannesburg CBD (1 mark)
A high-order central place offering specialised services.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the description 'Tall office buildings, banks, government departments and the highest land values' with the correct zone-letter (A, B, C, D, E, F or G) shown on Figure 1.2 — Concentric urban land-use model. (Refer to Figure 1.2 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: A — Central Business District (CBD) (1 mark)
Tall office buildings characterise the CBD.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the description 'Old factories, derelict buildings, low rents and overcrowding (urban decay)' with the correct zone-letter on Figure 1.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: B — Zone of transition / decay (1 mark)
Old factories and derelict buildings characterise this transition zone.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the description 'Warehouses, depots and small-scale manufacturing close to railways' with the correct zone-letter on Figure 1.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: C — Light industry / warehousing (1 mark)
Warehouses near rail line indicate the light industry zone.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the description 'Informal settlements, RDP houses and high population density' with the correct zone-letter on Figure 1.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: D — Low-income / informal housing (1 mark)
Informal settlements and RDP houses indicate the low-income residential zone.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the description 'Townhouse complexes and semi-detached homes for working professionals' with the correct zone-letter on Figure 1.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: E — Middle-income residential (1 mark)
Townhouses and semi-detached homes characterise the middle-income zone.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the description 'Large free-standing houses, gated estates and gardens for wealthy residents' with the correct zone-letter on Figure 1.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: F — High-income residential (1 mark)
Free-standing houses and gated estates characterise the high-income zone.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the description 'Small farms, country lodges and weekend retreats on the city edge' with the correct zone-letter on Figure 1.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: G — Rural-urban fringe / commuter zone (1 mark)
Country lodges and weekend retreats characterise the rural-urban fringe.

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term site with reference to settlement geography. (Refer to Figure 1.3 — A rural village with site factors and situation factors in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Site = the actual physical land/ground on which the settlement is built. It refers to the specific physical features of the location itself (soil, water, slope, drainage, shelter, etc.). (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term situation with reference to settlement geography.
subQuestions.memoText: Situation = the position of a settlement relative to surrounding features such as other towns, transport routes, markets, rivers and natural resources. It describes where the settlement is in the wider region. (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify what is represented by site factor labelled 1 on Figure 1.3.
subQuestions.memoText: Site factor 1 represents the water supply (the river running through the village). (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify what is represented by situation factors labelled 4 and 5 on Figure 1.3.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Situation factor 4 represents the road link to Town A (the local market). (1 mark)
Mark 2: Situation factor 5 represents access to the N3 highway / City B. (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why the position of the village in Figure 1.3 represents a favourable site. Refer to TWO site factors from the figure.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per fully-explained factor (factor + reason). Maximum 4.

Any TWO well-explained:
• Reliable water supply from the river — drinking, irrigation and livestock. (2 marks)
• Fertile farmland beside the village (gentle valley floor with deep soils) — supports crop production. (2 marks)
• Sheltered by hills — protection from strong winds and easier defensive position. (2 marks)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why the position of the village in Figure 1.3 represents a favourable situation. Refer to TWO situation factors from the figure.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per fully-explained factor. Maximum 4.

Any TWO well-explained:
• Road link to Town A = farmers can sell produce at the market. (2 marks)
• Highway link to City B = workers can commute and the village can access wider services and goods. (2 marks)
• Central position between three towns = strong trade catchment. (2 marks)

subQuestions.questionText: Rural depopulation is a major problem in many South African villages. Suggest TWO strategies that can be used to slow down rural depopulation.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO (1 mark each):
• Improve rural roads, electricity and water infrastructure.
• Build local clinics, schools and high schools so families do not need to leave.
• Promote agro-processing and rural tourism to create local jobs.
• Provide land-reform programmes and farmer-support to make small-scale farming viable.

subQuestions.questionText: Read off the percentage of South Africans living in urban areas in 2000. (Refer to Figure 1.4 — Percentage of South Africa's population living in urban areas, 1990–2030 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: 56,9% (accept any value 56–57%) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the percentage-point increase in urban population between 1990 and 2024. Show ALL working.
subQuestions.memoText:
Calculation:
Mark 1: Correct values identified — 2024 value = 68,7%; 1990 value = 52,0% (1 mark for correct values)
Mark 2: Increase = 68,7 − 52,0 = 16,7 percentage points (1 mark for correct subtraction with units / pp)

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term urbanisation.
subQuestions.memoText: Urbanisation is the increase in the proportion of a country's population living in urban areas (towns and cities), driven by rural-to-urban migration and natural population growth in cities. (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: State TWO pull factors that attract people from rural areas to South African cities.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO (1 mark each):
• More job opportunities in factories, offices and services.
• Better healthcare and hospitals.
• Better schools, colleges and universities.
• Reliable electricity, water and sanitation.
• Greater entertainment / lifestyle options.

subQuestions.questionText: State TWO push factors that drive people away from rural areas in South Africa.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO (1 mark each):
• Rural unemployment and lack of jobs.
• Drought, soil erosion or land degradation reducing farm output.
• Poor schools, clinics and infrastructure in rural areas.
• Mechanisation of farms reducing the need for farm labour.
• Poverty and limited access to land.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain how rapid urbanisation has contributed to the growth of informal settlements around major South African cities.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Rapid urbanisation creates demand for housing that cities cannot supply fast enough — demand exceeds supply. (1 mark)
Mark 2: Migrants build informal shacks on vacant land close to job opportunities (factories, CBD, transport hubs). (1 mark)
Mark 3: Without title deeds, no formal services (water, electricity, sewage) are provided, so the area grows organically into an informal settlement. (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest TWO sustainable strategies that municipalities can use to manage informal settlements rather than removing them.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per strategy. Maximum 4.

Any TWO of:
• In-situ upgrading — install services (water, electricity, sewage, roads) in existing settlements rather than removing them. (2 marks)
• Provide title deeds to current occupants so they can invest in their homes. (2 marks)
• RDP / FLISP housing programmes to gradually replace shacks with formal homes. (2 marks)
• Build community facilities (clinics, schools, parks) within the settlement. (2 marks)
• Skills training and small-business support to lift incomes. (2 marks)

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term urban renewal. (Refer to the extract 'Urban Renewal in South African Cities' in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Urban renewal = the deliberate process of upgrading or redeveloping run-down inner-city areas by repairing buildings, restoring infrastructure and attracting new businesses and residents. (Accept similar wording.) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Quote ONE example of an urban renewal project from the extract.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE of (1 mark):
• Maboneng precinct (Johannesburg)
• V&A Waterfront (Cape Town)
• Warwick Junction project (Durban)

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term gentrification in your own words.
subQuestions.memoText: Gentrification is the process where the character of a low-income neighbourhood changes when wealthier residents and businesses move in, rents and property values rise, and original poorer residents are displaced. (2 marks for clear definition with 'displacement' or 'pushing out original residents'.)

subQuestions.questionText: State ONE social and ONE economic challenge associated with gentrification.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark for naming a clear social challenge AND 1 for explaining; same for economic. Allow 1 'naming' mark only if explanation is missing.

Examples:
• Social: Original (low-income) residents lose their homes and community. (1 + 1 = 2 marks)
• Economic: Rents rise and small informal traders cannot afford to stay. (1 + 1 = 2 marks)
• Other social: cultural identity / heritage of the area is lost. (1 mark)
• Other economic: services aimed at the poor disappear. (1 mark)

Maximum 3.

subQuestions.questionText: In a paragraph of 8–10 lines, discuss the social, economic and environmental benefits of urban renewal in South African cities. Use evidence from the extract where appropriate. (Use Level 1–4 paragraph rubric.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Level 1–4 holistic rubric:
• Level 4 (7–8 marks): Comprehensive, well-structured response. Discusses ALL required dimensions in depth, uses correct terminology, integrates evidence from the figure/extract, reaches a clear conclusion. No factual errors.
• Level 3 (5–6 marks): Good response covering MOST required dimensions. Some use of evidence, generally correct terminology, minor errors. Conclusion present but may be brief.
• Level 2 (3–4 marks): Limited response covering ONE or TWO dimensions. Little use of evidence, vague language, several factual errors. No proper conclusion.
• Level 1 (1–2 marks): Very weak response. Off-topic in places, no evidence used, factually incorrect or copies the source verbatim. No structure.
• Level 0 (0 marks): No relevant response. Blank or completely off-topic.

Indicative content for full marks:

Social benefits:
• Restored sense of community pride and identity.
• Safer streets through more 'eyes on the street'.
• Mixed-income neighbourhoods reduce inequality.
• Cultural and recreational facilities (galleries, markets) create gathering spaces.
• Improved housing reduces homelessness.
• Cleaner streets and better lighting lower petty crime.

Economic benefits:
• New small businesses, restaurants and tourism create thousands of jobs.
• Rising property values increase municipal rates revenue.
• Lower cost than building greenfield infrastructure on the city edge.
• Greater foreign-tourist spending.
• Small traders gain a steady customer base.
• The city attracts investment because the inner-city is no longer perceived as 'dying'.

Environmental benefits:
• Reuse of existing buildings reduces demand for raw materials and limits urban sprawl onto farmland.
• Existing roads, water pipes and electricity networks are used more efficiently.
• Green public spaces and pavement upgrades improve air quality.
• Better waste management.
• Shorter commutes for inner-city workers reduce traffic emissions.

Conclusion (required for Level 4): A clear sentence stating that urban renewal, when carefully managed to avoid gentrification, delivers substantial social, economic AND environmental benefits to South African cities.

subQuestions.questionText: According to Figure 2.1, the sector contributing the largest share of South Africa's GDP is the … (Refer to Figure 2.1 — (a) GDP and (b) employment share by economic sector, South Africa 2024 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C tertiary sector (1 mark)
Figure 2.1(a) shows tertiary at 68% of GDP.

subQuestions.questionText: Which of the following is an example of a primary economic activity?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C Iron-ore mining (1 mark)
Mining is a primary (extractive) activity.

subQuestions.questionText: An example of a secondary activity is …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B operating a steel mill in Vanderbijlpark (1 mark)
Manufacturing/processing = secondary sector.

options.A: growing wheat in the Western Cape
options.B: operating a steel mill in Vanderbijlpark

subQuestions.questionText: The combined GDP contribution of the secondary and tertiary sectors in Figure 2.1 is …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D 90% (1 mark)
Secondary 22% + Tertiary 68% = 90%.

subQuestions.questionText: Beneficiation in the South African economy refers to …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B processing raw minerals into finished products before exporting (1 mark)
Beneficiation = adding value before export (e.g. refining platinum, smelting iron).

options.A: exporting minerals in their raw form
options.B: processing raw minerals into finished products before exporting

subQuestions.questionText: South Africa's economy is described as dualistic because it has …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B well-developed first economy alongside a struggling informal second economy (1 mark)
The defining feature of a dualistic economy.

options.B: a well-developed first economy alongside a struggling informal second economy

subQuestions.questionText: An SDI (Spatial Development Initiative) is best defined as …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C a development corridor linking economic nodes to boost growth (1 mark)
SDI = corridor approach (e.g. Maputo Development Corridor).

options.C: a development corridor linking economic nodes to boost growth
options.D: a new town built far from existing cities

subQuestions.questionText: The two largest container ports in South Africa, important for international trade, are …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B Durban and Cape Town (1 mark)
South Africa's two largest container ports.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the economic activity 'Heavy industry, financial services and Africa's largest stock exchange' with the correct centre-letter (A, B, C, D, E, F or G) shown on Figure 2.2 — Map of South Africa showing main economic centres. (Refer to Figure 2.2 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Answer: A — Gauteng (steel, vehicles, JSE) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Match the economic activity 'South Africa's main southern container port and a global tourism gateway' with the correct centre-letter on Figure 2.2.
subQuestions.memoText: Answer: B — Cape Town (port, manufacturing, tourism) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Match the economic activity 'East-coast container port, sugar refining and petro-chemical industries' with the correct centre-letter on Figure 2.2.
subQuestions.memoText: Answer: C — Durban (port, chemicals, sugar refining) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Match the economic activity 'Motor-vehicle assembly plants for VW, Ford and Mercedes-Benz' with the correct centre-letter on Figure 2.2.
subQuestions.memoText: Answer: D — Eastern Cape (motor manufacturing in Gqeberha and East London) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Match the economic activity 'Platinum and copper mining belt of the north-east' with the correct centre-letter on Figure 2.2.
subQuestions.memoText: Answer: E — Phalaborwa / Steelpoort (mining: platinum, copper) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Match the economic activity 'Iron-ore, manganese and diamond mining in the dry north-west' with the correct centre-letter on Figure 2.2.
subQuestions.memoText: Answer: F — Northern Cape (mining: iron-ore, manganese, diamonds) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Match the economic activity 'Wheat, deciduous fruit and wine grape farming in the south-west' with the correct centre-letter on Figure 2.2.
subQuestions.memoText: Answer: G — Western Cape interior (commercial agriculture: wheat, fruit, wine) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Read off the export value of citrus fruit from Figure 2.3. (Refer to Figure 2.3 — South Africa's top agricultural exports by value (USD billion), 2024 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: $1,85 billion (accept 1,8–1,9 b) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the combined export value of citrus fruit, wine and maize. Show ALL working.
subQuestions.memoText:
Calculation:
Mark 1: Correct values identified — Citrus = $1,85b + Wine = $1,05b + Maize = $0,92b (1 mark for correct values)
Mark 2: Total = $3,82 billion (1 mark for correct addition with units)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the dominant agricultural export shown in Figure 2.3.
subQuestions.memoText: Citrus fruit (highest export at $1,85b) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term food security.
subQuestions.memoText: Food security = a state in which all people, at all times, have physical, social and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food that meets their dietary needs and food preferences for an active and healthy life. (2 marks for full definition; 1 mark for partial.)

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss TWO ways in which climate change threatens agricultural production in South Africa.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per fully-explained way. Maximum 4.

Any TWO of:
• More frequent droughts reduce crop yields, especially maize and grain. (2 marks)
• Higher temperatures and heat stress kill livestock and damage fruit trees. (2 marks)
• Shifting rainfall patterns make planting/harvest timing unreliable. (2 marks)
• More pests and plant diseases spread in warmer conditions. (2 marks)
• Severe storms / flooding damage crops and topsoil. (2 marks)
subQuestions.topic: Economic Geography - Climate Change and Agriculture

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest TWO sustainable strategies that the government can implement to improve food security for vulnerable households.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per strategy. Maximum 4.

Any TWO of:
• Distribute drought-resistant seed varieties and provide irrigation subsidies. (2 marks)
• Promote community / school food gardens and urban agriculture. (2 marks)
• Maintain the National School Nutrition Programme and child-support grants. (2 marks)
• Build strategic grain reserves against bad seasons. (2 marks)
• Support small-scale and emerging farmers with training and finance. (2 marks)

subQuestions.questionText: State ONE benefit that agricultural exports bring to the South African economy.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE (1 mark):
• Foreign-exchange earnings
• Job creation
• Contribution to GDP
• Support for rural communities

subQuestions.questionText: Define an Industrial Development Zone (IDZ). (Refer to Figure 2.4 — Spatial Development Initiatives and Industrial Development Zones in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: An IDZ is a purpose-built, secured industrial estate located near a port or international airport that offers tax incentives, customs benefits and world-class infrastructure to attract export-oriented manufacturing. (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Define a Spatial Development Initiative (SDI).
subQuestions.memoText: An SDI is a development strategy that links existing economic nodes and underdeveloped regions along a transport corridor through coordinated investment in roads, rail and supporting industries. (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Name the IDZ labelled 1 and the IDZ labelled 4 on Figure 2.4.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: IDZ 1 = Coega IDZ (Gqeberha / Port Elizabeth). (1 mark)
Mark 2: IDZ 4 = Saldanha Bay IDZ. (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why most South African IDZs are located near major ports.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark for each clear reason. Maximum 2.

• Cheap, fast export of finished goods to world markets. (1 mark)
• Bulk import of raw materials at low transport cost. (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: State TWO physical (natural) factors that influence the location of an industry.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO (1 mark each):
• Flat / level land for buildings.
• Reliable water supply for cooling and processing.
• Suitable climate (mild, no extreme weather).
• Availability of raw materials nearby (minerals, agricultural produce).

subQuestions.questionText: State TWO human (economic) factors that influence the location of an industry.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO (1 mark each):
• Skilled and semi-skilled labour force.
• Good transport infrastructure (rail, port, airport, highways).
• Access to capital and finance.
• Large market / consumer demand.
• Government incentives, tax breaks and political stability.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss THREE benefits that IDZs bring to the surrounding region and to the South African economy.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any THREE (1 mark each):
• Job creation in the surrounding region.
• Inflow of foreign direct investment (FDI).
• Beneficiation — higher value-added exports rather than raw materials.
• Skills training and technology transfer to local workers.
• Increased tax revenue for government.
• Stimulates regional development and reduces inequality between metro and non-metro areas.

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest ONE challenge that IDZs face in attracting foreign investment.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE challenge (2 marks for clear explanation):
• Load shedding disrupts manufacturing schedules and raises costs. (2 marks)
• Crime and political instability reduce investor confidence. (2 marks)
• Skills shortage means firms must train staff or import skilled labour. (2 marks)
• Bureaucracy / policy uncertainty slows down approvals. (2 marks)

subQuestions.questionText: Quote ONE statistic from the extract that shows tourism's contribution to GDP. (Refer to the extract 'Tourism in South Africa' in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: R580 billion (any quote that captures the GDP-contribution figure). (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Quote the number of international tourist arrivals in 2025.
subQuestions.memoText: 9,7 million international tourists (in 2025). (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify TWO types of tourism mentioned in the extract.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of (1 mark each):
• Eco-tourism
• Township tourism
• Cultural heritage tourism

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss how load shedding negatively affects the tourism industry in South Africa.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any THREE (1 mark each). Maximum 3.

• Hotels, lodges and restaurants must run expensive diesel generators, raising costs. (1 mark)
• Attractions (museums, aquariums, lifts) close during outages — tourists feel cheated. (1 mark)
• Security risks rise (street lights, alarms off) — tourists fear crime. (1 mark)
• Reputation damage — negative reviews and word-of-mouth deter future visitors. (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: In a paragraph of 8–10 lines, discuss how South Africa can develop a more sustainable tourism industry. In your answer, suggest economic, environmental and social strategies. Use evidence from the extract where appropriate. (Use Level 1–4 paragraph rubric.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Level 1–4 holistic rubric:
• Level 4 (7–8 marks): Comprehensive, well-structured response. Discusses ALL required dimensions in depth, uses correct terminology, integrates evidence from the figure/extract, reaches a clear conclusion. No factual errors.
• Level 3 (5–6 marks): Good response covering MOST required dimensions. Some use of evidence, generally correct terminology, minor errors. Conclusion present but may be brief.
• Level 2 (3–4 marks): Limited response covering ONE or TWO dimensions. Little use of evidence, vague language, several factual errors. No proper conclusion.
• Level 1 (1–2 marks): Very weak response. Off-topic in places, no evidence used, factually incorrect or copies the source verbatim. No structure.
• Level 0 (0 marks): No relevant response. Blank or completely off-topic.

Indicative content for full marks:

Economic strategies:
• Diversify beyond the 'Big Five' attractions to spread visitor spending nationwide.
• Pursue BRICS-source markets through visa relaxation and direct flights.
• Invest in transport infrastructure (airports, roads, rail).
• Public-private partnerships for hotel and conference facilities.
• Market the country aggressively in 2025–2026 source-market campaigns.
• Support small B&Bs and tour operators with grants and skills training.

Environmental strategies:
• Channel tourism revenue into national parks and game reserves to fund conservation.
• Promote eco-lodges with renewable energy and water-recycling.
• Enforce 'no-trace' policies in protected areas.
• Cap visitor numbers at sensitive sites (Robben Island, Table Mountain summit).
• Plant indigenous gardens at lodges.
• Manage wastewater on the coast to protect marine ecosystems.

Social strategies:
• Township tourism partnerships that route a share of revenue back to local communities.
• Train local guides, chefs and lodge managers (rural skills development).
• Make heritage sites accessible and affordable to South Africans.
• Include local crafters and artists in tourist circuits.
• Respect cultural protocols at sacred sites.
• Tackle crime through visible tourism police in hot-spots.

Conclusion (required for Level 4): A clear sentence stating that combining economic, environmental AND social strategies is the only path to long-term sustainable tourism that benefits the South African economy without harming its ecosystems or communities.
